entities.summary:
Angilram of Metz was a Frankish prelate who played a pivotal role in the Frankish Empire during the 8th and 9th centuries. He served as the bishop of Metz from 768 until 791 and as the royal archchaplain under Charlemagne from 784 until 791.

As the bishop of Metz, Angilram was responsible for the conversion of the Saxons, a process that was instrumental in the expansion of Christianity in the region. He also played a key role in the construction of the Church of Saint Stephen in Metz, which became a major pilgrimage site. In addition, Angilram was a close advisor to Charlemagne and helped to mediate conflicts between the emperor and the Saxons.

Angilram's legacy extends beyond his own lifetime, as he played a significant role in shaping the political and religious landscape of the Frankish Empire. His efforts helped to establish Christianity as the dominant faith in the region, and his influence can still be seen in the architecture and art of the time.

In 792, Angilram attended the Council of Quierzy, where he played a key role in the adoption of the Carolingian capital of Aachen as the permanent seat of the Frankish Empire. This decision had far-reaching consequences for the development of Western Europe, as it helped to solidify the power of the Carolingian dynasty and paved the way for the rise of medieval kingdoms.

Angilram's life and legacy are a testament to the enduring power of faith and politics in shaping the course of human history.
